module.title: Meet BFS
goals: explain what BFS is for, and when it is the right tool
trace BFS by hand: say which vertex comes next, what is in the queue, which vertices are visited and the order they are visited in

segments.title: Quick recall: a graph in Python
When is BFS the right tool?
BFS step by step on the campus
Worked example: filling in a trace table
segments.body:
We trace BFS on the campus graph from **A**. One row per vertex that leaves the queue. A vertex is marked visited as soon as it **joins** the queue, so it is never added twice.

| Step | Current vertex | Queue after the step | Visited | Order so far |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | A | A | – |
| 1 | A | C, E | A, C, E | A |
| 2 | C | E, B, F | A, B, C, E, F | A, C |
| 3 | E | B, F, D | A, B, C, D, E, F | A, C, E |

**Step 1.** A leaves the queue and joins the order. Its neighbours in alphabetical order are C and E; neither is visited, so both join the back of the queue and are marked visited.

**Step 2.** C is at the front, so C leaves. Its neighbours are A, B, F. A is already visited; B and F join the queue.

**Step 3.** E leaves. Its neighbours are A, D, F. A is visited, and F is already visited (it is waiting in the queue), so only D joins.

The remaining steps work the same way. The full order is **A, C, E, B, F, D, G**.

activities.prompt: The walkways on campus can be used in both directions. What kind of graph is the campus map?

options.text: It is not a graph, because walkways have different lengths

feedback.correct: Right. A two-way connection is an undirected edge.
feedback.b: A directed edge only goes one way, like a one-way street. These walkways go both ways.
feedback.c: Edges can have lengths (weights) and still be a graph. Here we only care whether two buildings are connected.

hints: Think back to module 1: what is the difference between a directed and an undirected edge?
A directed edge has an arrow and can only be followed one way.
Can you walk from A to C and also from C to A? Then the edge has no single direction.
Answer: an undirected graph, because every walkway can be used in both directions.

activities.prompt: Using the `Graph` class from module 2, an empty undirected graph runs `add_vertex("A")`, `add_vertex("C")` and then `add_edge("A", "C")`. What is `adjacency` now?

feedback.correct: Right. An undirected edge is stored in both directions.
feedback.b: That is a directed edge from A to C. In an undirected graph C must also list A.
feedback.c: Each vertex maps to a list of neighbours, and both A and C are in the dictionary.

hints: Remember how module 2 stored an undirected edge.
Each vertex has a list of its neighbours.
If A is a neighbour of C, then C is also a neighbour of A.
Answer: {"A": ["C"], "C": ["A"]} — the edge is stored once in each vertex's list.

activities.prompt: You start at the Admin block (A). Which buildings can you reach by walking along exactly **one** walkway?

feedback.correct: Right. C and E are A's neighbours — the first ring BFS explores.
feedback.b: B is not joined to A. Count only the walkways that touch A.
feedback.c: F needs two walkways (A to C, then C to F).
feedback.d: Look again: A has two walkways, one to C and one to E.

hints: Find vertex A on the map.
Count the edges that touch A. Each one leads to a building one step away.
A has two edges.
Answer: C and E. They are A's neighbours.

activities.prompt: For each situation, choose whether BFS is a good fit and why.

left.text: Find the route between two stations on the Gautrain map with the fewest stops.
List everyone who is a friend, or a friend of a friend, of Thandi on a social network.
Add up the prices of all items in a shopping list.

right.text: Good fit: BFS reaches vertices in order of the fewest edges from the start.
Good fit: BFS explores one ring of neighbours at a time, so it finds everyone within two steps first.
Not a fit: there are no connections to follow, so this is not a graph problem.

feedback.s3: A list of prices has no vertices and edges to traverse. A simple loop is enough.
feedback.s1: Fewest stops means fewest edges. That is exactly the order in which BFS reaches vertices.
feedback.s2: Friends are one edge away, friends of friends two edges. BFS finds them ring by ring.

hints: First ask: are there things connected to other things? If not, it is not a graph problem.
BFS explores everything one edge away, then everything two edges away, and so on.
'Fewest stops' and 'friend of a friend' are both about counting edges from a start.
Answer: s1 → r1 (fewest stops), s2 → r2 (ring by ring), s3 → r3 (not a graph).

activities.prompt: A has been processed. The queue now holds **C, E** (front first). Which vertex does BFS process next?

feedback.correct: Right. C joined the queue first, so it leaves first.
feedback.E: E joined after C. A queue is first in, first out.
feedback.B: B is not in the queue yet. BFS only takes the vertex at the front of the queue.

hints: BFS always takes the next vertex from the queue.
A queue is first in, first out — like a line at the cafeteria.
Which of C and E joined the queue first?
Answer: C. It is at the front of the queue.

activities.prompt: BFS is now processing **C**. C's neighbours are A, B and F. Visited so far: A, C, E. Which vertices join the queue?

feedback.correct: Right. A is already visited, so only B and F join, in alphabetical order.
feedback.b: A is already visited. Adding it again would process it twice.
feedback.c: F is a neighbour of C too, and it is not visited yet.
feedback.d: G is not a neighbour of C. Only C's own edges count.

hints: Only neighbours of the current vertex can join the queue.
Skip any neighbour that is already visited.
C's neighbours are A, B and F. Which of them is in the visited set?
Answer: B and F. A is skipped because it is already visited.

activities.prompt: BFS is processing **E**. Its neighbours are A, D and F. The queue holds B, F, and F was marked visited when it joined. What happens to F?

options.text: Nothing. F is already visited, so it is skipped.
F joins the back of the queue again.
F moves to the front of the queue.

feedback.correct: Right. Marking F as visited when it joined the queue stops it being added twice.
feedback.b: Then F would be processed twice. That is the bug the visited set prevents.
feedback.c: BFS never reorders the queue. New vertices only join at the back.

hints: Look at the visited set. Is F in it?
A vertex is marked visited the moment it joins the queue.
BFS skips every neighbour that is already visited.
Answer: F is skipped. Only D joins the queue at this step.

activities.prompt: The visualiser pauses before each step. Pick the vertex BFS processes next.

feedback.wrong_not_front: BFS takes the vertex at the front of the queue. Look at the queue panel.
feedback.wrong_not_in_queue: That vertex has not joined the queue yet.
feedback.wrong_alphabetical: Alphabetical order only decides the order neighbours join the queue, not which vertex leaves next.

hints: Look at the queue panel, not the graph.
The vertex at the front of the queue joined earliest.
First in, first out: the leftmost vertex in the queue is next.
Answer for every step: the first vertex in the queue. The full order is A, C, E, B, F, D, G.

activities.prompt: Already confident? On the campus graph from A, after C is processed, what is in the queue (front first)?

feedback.correct: Correct — you can skip the worked example.
feedback.b: E was already waiting. New vertices join at the back, so E stays in front.
feedback.c: B and F join together at the back, after E.

hints: What was in the queue before C was processed?
C leaves from the front, and C's new neighbours join at the back.
Before: C, E. C leaves. B and F join behind E.
Answer: E, B, F.

activities.prompt: Trace BFS on this graph starting from **B**. Fill in one row each time a vertex leaves the queue. Mark a vertex visited when it joins the queue, and take neighbours in alphabetical order.

feedback.row_3_queue_has_C_twice: C was already visited when D was processed, so it does not join the queue again.
feedback.queue_order_wrong: New vertices join at the back of the queue, after the ones already waiting.
feedback.started_at_A: The start vertex is B this time, not A.
feedback.visited_missing_queued: A vertex is visited as soon as it joins the queue, not only when it is processed.

hints: Start with B in the queue and in the visited set. Row 1 is what happens when B leaves.
For each row: take the front of the queue, then add its unvisited neighbours in alphabetical order at the back.
Row 1: B leaves; its neighbours A and D join. Row 2: A leaves; its neighbours are B and C — only C is new.
Answer: order B, A, D, C, E. Queues after each row: [A, D], [D, C], [C], [E], []. At row 3, C is skipped because it is already visited.

activities.prompt: On the campus graph, what is the fewest number of walkways from the Admin block (A) to the Green (G)? Use the BFS order you found: A, C, E, B, F, D, G.

feedback.correct: Right: A → C → B → G. G was discovered from B, B from C, and C from A.
feedback.b: 6 is G's position in the order, not its distance. Follow who discovered whom back to A.
feedback.c: G is not joined to C or E. It needs one more walkway, from B.

hints: Ask: which vertex added G to the queue?
B added G. Which vertex added B?
C added B, and A added C. Count those walkways.
Answer: 3 walkways, A → C → B → G.
